name: Almodad
title: Joktan's firstborn son
summary: Almodad is the first of Joktan's thirteen sons and belongs to the lineage of Shem through Eber. He is listed in biblical genealogies as one of the ancestors of the peoples in the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula. The etymology of his name is disputed but is often interpreted as 'the immeasurable.' Almodad represents Joktan's branch of Eber's descendants—the line that did not lead to Abraham, but which, according to biblical tradition, gave rise to significant South Arabian ethnic groups.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in the genealogy of Shem
keyEvents.description: Almodad is listed as the firstborn son of Joktan in the genealogy following Shem, Noah's son.

keyEvents.title: Joktan's sons and their settlement areas
keyEvents.description: According to the text, Almodad and his brothers settled in the mountainous regions to the east, from Mesha to Sephar. This description marks the dispersion of Joktan's descendants after the flood.

keyEvents.title: Repetition in Chronicles
keyEvents.description: Almodad is mentioned again in 1 Chronicles as part of the great genealogy from Adam, confirming his place in biblical history.

keyEvents.title: Part of the Table of Nations
keyEvents.description: Almodad is part of the so-called 'Table of Nations' in Genesis 10, which describes how the nations of the earth spread after Noah's time.

keyEvents.title: Eber's two lines of descent
keyEvents.description: Almodad belongs to Joktan's line of Eber's descendants, unlike Peleg's line, which led further to Abraham. This shows the branching of the Semitic peoples.

versions.summary: Almodad was the firstborn son of Joktan and a grandson of Eber. He is mentioned in the Bible's genealogies as one of the ancestors of the Arab peoples. His name may mean 'the immeasurable' or 'God's friend', and he is regarded as the forefather of a people in the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula.
versions.title: Joktan's firstborn son
versions.reason: [minor] The sentence "His name may mean "the immeasurable" or "God's friend"" contains an uncertain etymology. "God's friend" is a less common interpretation. The most common explanation links the name to Arabic and means "the immeasurable" or "one who cannot be measured." It is better to be more cautious with alternative interpretations.; [minor] The role "patriarch" is acceptable, but "ancestor" would have been more precise for a person primarily known as the origin of a people rather than as a central patriarchal figure in salvation history.; [major] Footnotes are missing. For a figure like Almodad, information should be included about the etymology of the name, possible geographical identifications of the people he founded, and any connection to South Arabian inscriptions.; [minor] The description says "the flood" – the more precise Norwegian expression in a biblical context is "the great flood" or "Noah's flood."

versions.summary: Almodad was the firstborn son of Joktan and a grandson of Eber in Shem's lineage. He is mentioned in the biblical genealogies as one of the ancestors of the Arab peoples. The etymology of his name is uncertain, but it is most often linked to the meaning 'the immeasurable'. Almodad is regarded as the forefather of a people in the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula, and he belongs to Joktan's line – unlike Peleg's line, which led further to Abraham.

Otherwise, the list of siblings appears correct with 12 brothers (Joktan had 13 sons in total).

footnotes.text: The name Almodad (Hebrew: אַלְמוֹדָד, 'Almôdāḏ) has uncertain etymology. The most common interpretation links it to Arabic and gives the meaning 'the immeasurable' or 'one who cannot be measured'. Some scholars have also suggested a connection with South Arabian words for 'friend' or 'beloved'.

Several scholars have attempted to identify Almodad's descendants with tribes in South Arabia (modern-day Yemen). The Arab geographer Ya'qut al-Hamawi mentions a people called 'al-Mudad' in Yemen, which may possibly be linked to Almodad. This aligns with the biblical description of Joktan's sons settling in the eastern mountainous regions.

The Table of Nations in Genesis 10 is a unique document in the ancient world. It categorizes known peoples according to lines of descent and provides a theological perspective on the origin and spread of nations. Joktan's thirteen sons, including Almodad, are consistently linked to the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula.

The distinction between Peleg's line (which leads to Abraham and the people of Israel) and Joktan's line (which leads to the South Arabian tribes) is theologically significant. It shows that the biblical narrative is consciously selective: it follows one specific line (Peleg–Abraham) while acknowledging that other branches of Shem's descendants also developed into significant peoples.

Archaeological findings from the South Arabian region, including inscriptions from the ancient Sabaean kingdom and neighboring states, have revealed tribal names that may be connected to several of Joktan's sons. Although a direct link to Almodad has not been definitively proven, these findings support the general picture of an early Semitic presence in South Arabia.

In Jewish tradition (Midrash and rabbinic literature), Joktan's sons have often been regarded as the ancestors of the South Arabian and eastern peoples. Josephus (Antiq. 1.6.4) identifies Almodad with a people called 'Almodadei' without specifying an exact location, but places them generally in southern Arabia.
